newsitem.title: USA: Louisiana-Pacific to close pulp mill, take charge.
newsitem.headline: Louisiana-Pacific to close pulp mill, take charge.

text.p: Louisiana-Pacific Corp. said Monday it will close its Ketchikan pulp mill in southeast Alaska next year after the failure of negotiations with the Clinton administration over timber supply.
The company said it planned to take a $350 million pre-tax charge in the third quarter, or $215 million or $2 per share after taxes, to reflect the shutdown and other items.

The closing of the 48-year-old plant, which had been expected, will idle about 500 workers in Ketchikan, where Louisiana-Pacific is the city's largest employer. There are about 15,000 people in the Ketchikan area.
The target date for the shutdown is March 24, 1997.

Louisiana-Pacific attributed the shutdown to the "failure to reach a satisfactory agreement with the Clinton Administration to restore the original terms of the Ketchikan pulp mill's timber supply contract.

The company said unilateral changes to the contract by the U.S. Forest Service in 1991 led to "significant operating losses for the mill." The portion of the reserve related to the closure is $188 million. Through the first nine months of this year, the pulp operations lost an estimated $40 million.

Louisiana Pacific said Ketchikan Pulp will enter into immediate negotiations with the Department of Agriculture to determine the feasibility of continuing to run its two sawmills in southeast Alaska for two more years.

Under an agreement worked out by the White House and Alaska Sen. Frank Murkowski, Louisiana-Pacific said it expected to get enough timber to continue operating two sawmills in the region for two more years, employing 400 to 500 workers.
The company also said it planned in the fourth quarter to close or sell several plants which are no longer competitive or essential to its operations.

"Our goal is to adjust our capacity to meet what we believe will be the future demand for our current products," the company said. "A final announcement on exactly which plants will be closed will be made in the next 30-60 days."

Louisiana-Pacific also said it has agreed in principle to settle, on behalf of all defendants, all outstanding shareholder securities class action claims brought against the company and four of its former and current officers last year.

The suits currently are pending in the federal court in Portland, Ore. and stem from a drop in Louisiana Pacific's stock price following media and analyst accounts on May 25, 1995 of certain threatened or pending civil and criminal actions against the company.
The defendants agreed to the settlement without admitting any liability. The settlement calls for a payment of $65 million, of which about $20 million will be covered by insurance, the company said.
The after-tax cost of the uninsured portion is about $28 million, or 26 cents per share, which will be accrued in the third quarter.

In addition, the company said it intends to reserve an additional $117 million in the third quarter for anticipated costs associated with other outstanding litigation and claims, and for anticipated costs of shutting down and disposing of certain non-essential plants and equipment.
